utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we start, there is a few things I would like to mention. The first one is that this Trial Chamber has made a decision granting the applications for ex parte hearing. The time will be tomorrow afternoon, 3.00. The second matter is that there are still some motions which we are waiting for the response from the Prosecution. We hope the Prosecution could file their response as soon as possible. Well, Mr. Krsnik, I think you owe us an apology since you are late.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, of course, I do apologise. I was first late because of the traffic, and then I had to look through the tapes. So that is why I was 15 minutes late, and I really do apologise to everybody in the courtroom and outside it for being late. I hope you'll accept my apologies. Thank you. May I begin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, unless I'm mistaken, I think I left off yesterday in the portion of my opening statement in which I was talking about some facts which the Defence will provide evidence of, to prove, with witnesses as well, and I think I was referring to conflicts between the Muslims -- or rather a part of the Muslim people in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I think my last sentence yesterday was recognition of the fact that in that war conflict, unfortunately, there were people who were abused and beaten and tortured of all three -- belonging to all three ethnic groups, but as a very sad fact of and consequence of a war conflict, of a lack of education, lack of organisation, and military discipline, disciplines, and military operations. And I think I left off yesterday by saying the following, that the fact of implementing ethnic cleansing was a consequence of the armed conflict, an inescapable consequence of the armed conflict, a consequence in which everybody fell victim, and in which individual crimes and ethnic cleansing, or crimes, were not the objective, not an aim in themselves, but an unfortunate consequence in which the criminal has his full name, his first and last name, and we can't call -- refer to them as a Croat or a Serb or a Muslim, because a people is never a criminal. The Defence will show that there was no persecution of Muslims. They were not sacked from their jobs. The Muslims who had jobs and were employed in institutions or enterprises, economic ones, and who were able to function, who were able to work, remained in their work posts, the ones they had occupied before the conflict. We are going to show that the Muslims -- that it was precisely the Party of Democratic Action that exerted pressure on the Muslims themselves to leave their positions, not to cooperate with, and not to participate in, and not to become employed within, the HVO because, as you know, the HVO was an organisation of both civilian authority and military authority. It was both civil and military. Contrary to the assertions of the Prosecution that the HVO units launched an attack first, the Defence will show and demonstrate before this Trial Chamber and present evidence which say that it was the BiH army which attacked the HVO and that this happened on the 9th of May, 1993 and that the conflict which followed in no case did it target Muslim civilians. The Defence is duty-bound to present evidence and proof to show that the Croatian army neither was nor did it occupy -- and I'm talking about Mostar now. It did not occupy Mostar, and the genesis of the conflict of the so-called Bosnia-Herzegovina army and the HVO, the genesis of that conflict, especially in Mostar, that that was where its origins were, and we will show that Mladen Naletilic himself was not an individual who waged a campaign against the Muslims. The Defence will also present evidence to challenge the claims made that the events in Mostar, Sovici, and Doljani had as their aim ethnic cleansing, and the assumption of control over Mostar and Jablanica, those two municipalities, as well as other municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in order to force the Muslims to leave the territory which they had inhabited up until then. We shall, of course, present evidence and proof to show that my client, Mladen Naletilic, in no way acted with those intentions. And this brings me to the part of the indictment that we have to challenge as the Defence, and of course we will be doing so, and that is the Convicts Battalion and that issue. The Prosecution claims that Mladen Naletilic throughout the material time in this indictment was commander of the Convicts Battalion and that the Convicts Battalion held 200 to 300 soldiers grouped in several sub-units and that those sub-units were called the ATJ or ATG, which means anti-terrorist group or anti-terrorist unit, with bases in the municipalities of Mostar, Siroki Brijeg, and Ljubuski. According to the indictment and the position taken by the Prosecution, the main tasks of the Convicts Battalion were combat missions on the front line, expulsions and attacks against Bosnian Muslim civilians in the territories under, as the Prosecution claims, HV and HVO occupation, and that the Convicts Battalion, or the KB, acted as part of or in coordination with the HVO and HV. Your Honours, the Defence will call witnesses who have direct knowledge of the events that took place, and they will be speaking precisely about the Convicts Battalion itself. These witnesses will not be second-hand witnesses, Your Honours. The Defence will present evidence to show that Mladen Naletilic was not the commander of the KB throughout the time, that is to say, at all times material to this indictment, and certainly - and you will be witness to this - that the Defence will call a number of witnesses to show that he was not the main and highest authority either in the HV or the HVO. What the Defence is going to prove is that the Convicts Battalion was established and came into being and that at the beginning only had 10 to 20 young men, and at the end of the Serb aggression, it grew to become a unit with 200 to 300 young men. After the demobilisation took place and after the war ended with the Army of Republika Srpska - and this was in December 1992 - and with the departure of the demobilised young men back to Croatia or back to Germany, where they were living and working, a part of them, and the other part to their -- back to their own homes in Bosnia-Herzegovina, without expecting a conflict, especially not a conflict with the Bosnia-Herzegovina army, the HVO attempted to create or to train as the start of some professional units or special purpose units as more elite smaller units within the HVO. So, for example, we have the emergence of the anti-terrorist group, the ATG, and it came -- it was born from under the wings of the young men in the KB, the Convicts Battalion, who had been in the war in 1992. They were members of the Convicts Battalion, so they were born from under their wings. And the Baja Kraljevic anti-terrorist group was formed, and it led a soldier's life, which means that they would get up in the morning, salute the flag, have their regular training and exercise in the morning, and everything else that is considered to be the life of a soldier, and they lived in the barracks on the Heliodrom. But within this HVO organisation, it was an independent unit, an autonomous unit, and it received orders from its commander on a daily morning basis. And the Defence will move to prove, in due course, that when it was called to intervene as a unit, as a special-purpose unit, which -- when the front line has to be broken through or when the enemy has broken through the front line and when it is required to act, then it is called in, and it is commanded by the zone commander himself, by the immediate zone commander or the commander of the brigade, or rather the battalion or company, which at that particular moment in time is at the front line. And not only the Baja Kraljevic group but any anti-terrorist group or unit or special-purposes unit and intervention unit would be at that given moment. Your Honours, we are going to present evidence, first and foremost here, to show that the Convicts Battalion existed only in Siroki Brijeg with the old veterans, if I can use that term, those dating back to 1991 and 1992, those veterans, who lived in their own homes at Siroki Brijeg or perhaps at the Siroki Brijeg Hotel and that they never numbered -- this unit never numbered more than about 80 people, 80 men, who had rallied together, who rallied together when there was -- when the sound for danger was sounded, and they would rally at the -- as the Baja Kraljevic ATG did, the only difference being that the Convicts Battalion in Siroki Brijeg did not carry out a soldier's life, the life of a soldier in a barracks, if I can put it that way. They did not have any daily briefings, they did not rally every morning for their exercises, et cetera, but we will come to that in due course and demonstrate that through the evidence that we shall present. Therefore, Your Honours, it is very important - it is especially important for the Defence, and we shall endeavour to do so at all times - to give you a picture and to help you understand and differentiate between one unit called the Convicts Battalion, one single unit, and possibly some other groups that are called either anti-terrorist groups or special-purpose units or whatever they may be - the Vinko Skrobo, Benko Penavic, Zeljko Bosna, they all had different names - but they had nothing to do with the Convicts Battalion or its internal organisation and establishment. And this brings me to a situation which the Prosecution claims and refers to the Juka Prazina unit, was under the command of my client, that is what the Prosecution has claimed. Your Honours, we will present evidence and proof to show who Mr. Jusuf Prazina was, nicknamed Juka. I am not going to dwell on his curriculum vitae, but what you should know at this point in time is the following. Mr. Alija Izetbegovic personally appointed this gentleman commander of all the special units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, at that time in occupied Sarajevo, and he was rapidly to come into conflict not only with Mr. Izetbegovic himself but also with the so-called military professionals of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army in Sarajevo, and his unit at that particular time was the most numerous one and the best organised one within the Bosnia-Herzegovina army, and numbered over 5.000 men. So the conflict came about, on the one side, through fear and the fear of Mr. Prazina and the influence that he could wield in the position that he held, on the one side, and on the other side, Mr. Prazina insisted upon the fact that Sarajevo should be liberated first and then together with everybody who had Bosnia in their hearts, should start liberating - and I say this in inverted commas - should liberate Bosnia and create Bosnia as a future community of all three ethnic groups, all three nations. We are going to provide evidence, Your Honours, to show what the situation was like around him. We're going to bring witnesses who were with him throughout that time and who together with him after the conflict went to Herzegovina. And we will, of course, prove, Your Honours, that the Party of Democratic Action, or rather, its president, Alija Izetbegovic, did not allow nor did he want to hear about any plans to liberate Sarajevo coming from the HVO. Without entering into an analysis of this situation -- and time will tell. And the judges of history along with God's judgement is the most just judgement of all. And because of all the suffering that ensued as a consequence of the situation for all people who lived in Sarajevo -- and we're going to show that Sarajevo could have been liberated after a period of two months, two months into the occupation. I think that history and God will be the judges of those and to those who use Sarajevo as propaganda - that was on the CNN news for three years - in order to realise their political goals, falsely depicting the situation and the victims and casualties or creating the image of only one type of victim, a victim on one side. As I say, this could have been reduced to three months, two to three months. And during that time, Sarajevo could have been liberated. Your Honours, let me now concentrate and focus on the specific counts in the indictment. And I'll start off with Mostar, the 9th of May, 1992. Your Honours, I don't want to tire you today with that because we will be presenting witnesses to talk about Mostar and what happened prior to the conflict in -- on the 5th of May, 1993. But what I wanted to say -- I do want to say is that we're going to show that the BH army did have plans, did issue orders, which we're going to show here, as early on as the 16th of April, 1993, in which it elaborated a plan of attack and occupation of Mostar, conditionally speaking, because you can't occupy a town of the people living there. You can't occupy my street or my river or my tree, if we're talking about the local inhabitants of Mostar. Today it is a common city, a joint city. A Berlin Wall was never erected there, if I can use the comparison. It is still a city of the people who live there. During the night, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the night between the 8th and the 9th -- may I ask for the Court's indulgence for a moment and your attention, please. If you recall that this is the Bulevar. I don't know if the ELMO is switched on. Do you have the map on your screens? The BH army on the night between the 8th and the 9th, they crossed this line in Mostar, in the town of Mostar. And with their special units, special purpose units -- and we'll show that members of the BH army came from all over Bosnia-Herzegovina. For example, special units, the Jusuf Prazina, nicknamed Zuka, his special unit. Then there was -- there were other ones. And they came to the roundabout here. And the object was to join up and to reach the Zagrebacka or Kalemova Street and join with Vranica, while the other units went to take control of Balinovac. And had they succeeded in doing that, the town of Mostar would have fallen into their hands straight away. Now, how did the attack actually begin? At a preordained sign in the morning, at 3.00, 4.00, or 5.00, a sniper from the Vranica building killed a policeman -- and his surname was Lugonja. He was doing his daily duty. He was in uniform, on the beat, on the job. And the Defence will demonstrate that to this Trial Chamber and provide its evidence and proof. After that -- and let me also say that up until the 9th of May, there was no demarcation line or confrontation line in Mostar at all. But the battle began for each building at each street. But it was only on the 10th, or rather, the 9th in the afternoon and the evening on the 9th and the morning of the 10th, the morning of the 10th of May, all morning, the HVO units who were stationed in Mostar, the 2nd, 3rd, 4th Battalion, as they were called, and the commanders of the brigades in which these battalions -- of which these battalions were commanded per and in part. We're going to bring in those commanders here into the courtroom. And as eyewitnesses, they will be able to tell you what happened; as well as the people who had been taken prisoner on the 9th of May and the 10th of May, around this Rondo, round point, in that locality. Some of them were freed in a counterattack, but others were taken into detention, across the Bulevar, across the Neretva River, to be imprisoned for ten days; others for one month; and others only in 1994. As for example, some evidence that we're going to put forward here, that the parish priest of the cathedral was taken into custody and detained in that way. And it was only at the intervention of the Vatican itself, was exchanged -- later to be exchanged, and when he was pulled out of the eastern part of Bosnia, we are going to show this beyond all doubt, he was killed on the eastern side, this parish priest. He was an officer of the Spanish army, who was -- that is to say this officer of the Spanish army, who was a member of UNPROFOR at the time. Your Honours, I have been told by my colleagues that the transcript says that the parish priest was killed. It was not the parish priest. It was the officer of the Spanish army who was killed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the action was launched to pull out the parish priest from detention, from prison, from the left to the right bank of the River Neretva. And through all due respect, every year, to commemorate his death, in Medjugorje, at his grave, a mass is held. And I'm not clear today what the indictment and Prosecution wanted to say by presenting evidence in that regard. That is why we have done our best, Your Honours, that the people who participated in those events should be your witnesses and should come here into this courtroom to tell what -- to tell us what actually happened. Your Honour, I would just like to tell you -- give you a few details which you will certainly be interested in and these are details we will present in this Tribunal. We will present evidence to prove that (redacted) was in Vranica, but not as a civilian but as a commander at the time, and when the plan failed on the 10th, that is to say when the units of the BH army were pushed back to the Bulevar, from that date, the 9th of May, this famous Bulevar became the confrontation line, the demarcation line right up until the Washington Agreement. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [redacted] the Vranica building, and a surrender was carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I'm a little worried, Mr. Krsnik, about what you're saying now - [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can go into closed session. I will immediately explain what it is about. I never said who the witness was. I'm only speaking about the names of the people who participated in those events. I mentioned a lot of names, but I never said, and I will never mention, who the witness was or the name of the witness, but these are the names of the people, of a series of people, who unfortunately participated on all sides in the history of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And who the witness was, I never said that, and it wouldn't cross my mind to say such a thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I may be mistaken, Mr. Krsnik, but the name at line - I'm no good at reading this - 1409;48:33, was that not a protected witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we go into a private session now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think we better go to private session for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I certainly won't mention names any more. I shall do my best not to do. So I'll just focus on the events. The event is important. And that was on the 9th of May, 1993 in Mostar. The Defence shall provide irrefutable evidence by calling witnesses and will show how an attempt at deception was made and we shall prove how the HVO attacked for no reason -- an attempt was made to prove how the HVO attacked for no reason in the Vranica building, which is in the centre of town and the only reason being to take one more building. I didn't -- I couldn't see any other reasons. So our witnesses, Your Honours, will say what happened exactly here, and they will talk about all the people who in the attempt to capture Mostar were captured, were taken away from their flats in the west of Mostar and, as I said, right up to -- have a look once more. I will show you where -- how far they got. They crossed the Bulevar. And this is where they arrived. This is where Vranica is. Some of the units even reached Balinovac. And then in a two-day fight, there was a fight for houses, for streets. They were pushed back, and they came to the Bulevar. They reached the Bulevar. And since then, the Bulevar has been the demarcation line -- the Bulevar was the demarcation line. And now, Your Honours, we will show you that up until the 13th of June, there really was nothing else happening, nothing. For two months, there was absolute peace, absolute peace in Mostar. Why? Because there were peace initiatives which had been started by all sides, both by the International Community, by the Croatian president, and by the sides involved in the conflict themselves. And when did the conflict start again? Again, this was an attack - and this is something that has been recognised in the indictment too - an attack by the BH army against the northern camp. And they called it liberation. I don't know in whose name they were liberating it and from whom. And this camp was on the eastern side. It was on the other side of the River Neretva. And while doing this, they liberated Croats from their homes, and they took them into captivity to Bijelo Polje, Vrapcici. These were all municipalities of the town of Mostar, on the east or left bank. They founded a number of camps on the left bank, the well-known building of the SDK, the 4th primary school, the primary school in Bijelo Polje, where during 1993 -- throughout 1993 and right up until 1994 in March, civilians too - about 80 per cent were civilians - were kept in detention by the BH army there. Unfortunately - and I will always refer to this - when they say "we liberated" something, well, they liberated -- well, whether it was a Muslim or a Croat and had been living in the municipality of Mostar for 200 years, who did they liberate him from? They liberated him from himself, just because he was a Croat. I think this is very hypocritical to say that the BH army was liberating Bosnia. Perhaps they were liberating Bosnia. But the territory which they were going to take, which they were going to seize and Islamise, yes, in that manner, yes; in those terms, yes, they were liberating it from members of other faiths or of other peoples; in that sense, yes, they really were liberating it. I would now ask the technician to show us the videotape. I think it's still tape number 1. I don't know if we have contact with the technical booth. Could you please ... Please, could you fast-forward it a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need the second supplement, not this one. Could you stop here for a moment, please. So after the 9th of May, there was a peace initiative. This came from Dr. Franjo Tudjman. And it first started by providing Alija Izetbegovic and Mate Boban with a message. And finally following his initiative, on the 18th of May, in Medjugorje, representatives of the International Community and all the sides of the conflict met. And Franjo Tudjman was at the head of the Croatian delegation. Alija Izetbegovic headed the Muslim delegation. And on behalf of the International Community, there was Mr. Owen, Mr. Stoltenberg. The representative of the European Community, I think it was Mr. Jenson. The UNPROFOR commander, I think his name was General Wahlgren. Could we please show this part. Could you fast-forward a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are various quotations here, messages. Could you stop here for a bit. Please could you stop the videotape and could you rewind it a bit. Stop here. Stop it here. So this part is the one I need, the one that comes after this image here, and the one which concludes it -- let's start here. And we need the sound too, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] The Spanish officer who tragically died, there was a mass for him in Medjugorje. And the Mostar bishop gave this mass. The officer of the battalion died while he was being taken out of captivity. Following the tragic death of the Spanish officer, the commander of the Spanish Battalion expressed his condolences -- was given the condolences by Mate Boban. The fate of the Croats who have been surrounded in the municipality of Konjic is still not sure. There are still Croatian villages which are surrounded by Muslims and have been surrounded for over a month. Well-known diplomats arrived at the airport. This was a matter of considerable interest, and there were representatives of the media. They gathered here, following the initiative from Dr. Franjo Tudjman. They were speaking about how to put an end to the unnecessary conflict between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croats, the HVO in Mostar, in Northern Herzegovina, and in Central Herzegovina -- Central Bosnia. So how to stop the conflict in the provinces which should belong to the Croats according to the Vance-Owen Plan. David Owen was there and the Norwegian diplomat Stoltenberg was present too. [In English] ... in Mostar and around these areas stopped. [Voiceover] We want to see an end to this conflict. We want to see the HVO and the BH army. We want to see this conflict stopped between them. We want to find a political solution which will enable them to live as partners, which will enable these constituent peoples to live as partners. They shave the municipalities of Travnik and Vranica. This is how we have to speak with everyone, and we don't want to see anyone in captivity. The public wasn't present at the talks. And in one case, Alija Izetbegovic wasn't present when Tudjman was there. So the usual messages for the public were not present, and we had to rely on the participants' announcements. Alija Izetbegovic arrived at the airport and said that he wasn't an optimist. This is all he said. And before flying to Medjugorje, when he spoke to the Russian minister of the foreign office and to Stoltenberg and Pederson he didn't change his mood. And in response to the journalists, he just remained -- in response to journalists' questions, he remained silent. Tudjman commented on what Izetbegovic had said yesterday, and he said that the HVO units were paramilitary units. This is what was claimed. This is quite incredible. It's hard to understand how such a conclusion can be reached, given that Mr. Izetbegovic signed a document where he spoke about the fact that the HVO was a regular army. Not a paramilitary formation, just as regular as the BH army. And it is a well-known fact that the HVO prevented the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina from falling into the hands of the greater Serbian policies. This is a document that he signed, and our friendship was based on this and our cooperation was based on this. And this is quite incomprehensible. And we shall try to address this in our talks today and to reestablish relations between Croatia and Bosnia. Neils Pederson was not at all talkative. He came to give the viewpoint of the 12 members of the European Union. Koziraf [phoen] said, "The situation is difficult, but it's not terrible. What is important is that all the people that we have spoken to, including Izetbegovic, Tudjman, and all of them spoke about the validity of the Vance-Owen Plan, and they admitted the possibility of implementing it in a progressive way. We'll meet in Belgrade with the Serbian side, that is to say, the Yugoslav side. And afterwards we will have close consultations with others. Later we will have detailed talks with our American partners." In response to the question how would Vance Owen's plan be implemented, he said -- Koziraf said, "I have close contacts with the American secretary. We spoke last night. And I intend to maintain these close contacts. Please don't think that there could be any disagreement. However, it is agreed that the Croatian president was the greatest victor here, and the commander of the UNPROFOR forces confirmed this too, the Swedish General, Eric Wahlgren. Tudjman is the host, yes. He invited us to this meeting. And I might perhaps be the host in the command of the French Battalion. All the participants went to Medjugorje from Split. Yes, representatives of the Croatian people arrived in Medjugorje today. It was a meeting suggested by Dr. Franjo Tudjman. Lord Owen was also there" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Stop there, please. [Interpretation] I have been warned not to show lengthy videotapes in the course of my opening statement. And -- but you have seen some of the tapes, and this is my first opening statement. And I think that brief photographs and images should be shown. But I think that you have been able to see Dr. Franjo Tudjman and the events that were filmed. But the participants of the meeting will come and testify here, and we hope to show that despite what was happening this time in Mostar, that is to say on the 9th of May, initiatives never ceased to bring the conflict to an end, and this was one attempt, the attempt in Medjugorje, to ensure that the conflicting parties, the Muslims and the Croats in this particular case, be stopped, or to prevent them from starting again, especially as the Vance-Owen Plan was to enter its -- the stage of application. It was signed by both the Croats and the Muslims. But there were constant obstructions, and now it becomes clear why we or why anybody signing a peace plan of any kind on several occasions never actually wants to implement it in the field. At that meeting, it was the will to implement the Vance-Owen Plan was reiterated and to release all the prisoners, all for all, on the principle of all for all, and on that occasion, everybody was released, all those who were brought into the so-called camp, some people referred to it as a camp, others to refer to it as a collection centre, in the prison building, which was in the one-time JNA barracks, which are referred to and called the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but could you inform me how long are you going to take? If you could finish your opening statement in 15 minutes, we will go on, but if not, we will have our break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll need half an hour at the most, perhaps 15 minutes but half an hour at the most. I go to Mostar, to Sovici and Rastani, with which I conclude my opening statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll have our break and we'll resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, I have had a few consultations during the break and I think I can say that I will be over in approximately half an hour. I have made some adjustments. We were talking about Medjugorje and the peace efforts and the agreement that was reached in Medjugorje, and on the basis of that agreement, from the collection centre or camp or whatever you like to call it that was called the Heliodrom, all those were released except those who were ascertained to be members of the BH army, and we are going to show you through our evidence that there were exactly 599 of them, army members. This figure I have quoted because there were lists, even when they were a joint army, and those members who were not from Mostar but who had come from different parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina and whom people didn't know, they of course had to go through a phase of examination, to see where they had come from and who they were, and this is natural in every military procedure. The courts were functioning and there was a military court that was established, which conducted investigations and legal proceedings, and we will demonstrate that about 600 individuals were processed in this way, and the judgements by the investigating court in Mostar prescribed for detention. So they were not punished only because they were Muslims, as they would have you believe, but because they put -- took part in an armed conflict. Some were suspected of having looted, pilfered, burnt and so on. So that is why they were held in detention and sent to the prison in Ljubuski or the military court sent him to the Heliodrom. Your Honours, if there is fighting for every building and every street, can you imagine the situation in a high-rise building, where the inhabitants are Muslims, Croats and Serbs all living together? He surely wouldn't have taken children who were between -- who were five and eight years old there if he had wanted to be in command. He wouldn't have taken his children there and then gone into combat. And we will call witnesses to prove this here, to prove that this is the truth. But when he saw what was happening, he was afraid for his children, and there were lots of people at Risovac. Everybody went and asked what was going on, what was happening, but it was only when the shooting started, because until then there wasn't any shooting every -- there were members of the army moving back and forth, there were people moving back and forth. That was not unusual. What was unusual was when the shooting started. And then people asked themselves what was going on. They went to see what was going on. And the witnesses will show whether Mr. Naletilic went personally or whether somebody came to tell him, not only him but to the inhabitants, that the battles were starting, that the fighting was starting, and that people had begun to leave the area when they learnt what was going on. And he continued his stay. He stayed on, although he intended to leave on Sunday, and he was always very much concerned about the young men in the Convicts Battalion, because they were all children of his friends. So you can imagine what it's like to go to somebody's house and say that somebody's son had been killed, and to say that, "I was the commander, wasn't the commander, or I mobilised him," or whatever. It takes guts to go to a parent and tell them that their child had been killed. He never -- he always carried out that responsibility because he always considered himself to be responsible for the establishment of the Convicts Battalion in the first place, so that whenever a young man was killed, he always had the moral responsibility to attend that young person's funeral and to inform the parents personally, because you know in Siroki Brijeg, it's a small place and everybody knows each other, and that's precisely what happened. On the 19th or the 20th - I can't remember exactly; the witnesses will be more specific and tell you the dates - but that was when two members were killed. Two had been killed previously straight away on the 17th, and two others were killed a few days later. Or rather the two people who were killed were not members of the Convicts Battalion. They were members of some of the HVO units. But on the 19th and 20th, two persons were killed - I won't state their names now; I'll do so in due course - he was informed up there that that had happened, and as he always did, regardless of which position my client, Mladen Naletilic, was in, he would go personally. He took up that dead young man, transported him to Siroki Brijeg. And this was the 19th or the 20th. The action was already over, and had it not been, it would have ceased, because that was the custom throughout the HVO, to pick up the dead, the friends, the relatives, there were always friends and relatives who were just one or two kilometres in front of their own houses because they were all defending their own villages and their own houses. I apologise. I see the time. I promised to finish within half an hour. I've gone on further. But, Your Honours, we will prove that the Convicts Battalion was never in Sovici, especially Mr. Mladen Naletilic had nothing to do with it, and we'll see what position he held at the time, which leaves me another ten minutes. I think I'll be able to finish within ten minutes. Because this -- I want to say that it is the responsibility of the Defence to show Mladen Naletilic as he is, the man he is. I am not behaving in front of this Tribunal as I would generally in my practice as a lawyer. This is a new thing for all of us. But it is a top-level Tribunal, so I'm going to put everything before you, even things that are not to my advantage. I'm not going -- I'm going to tell the truth, even if some of those things are not very pleasant to hear. Let them be heard. They are the truth. So I'm going to depict my client, Mladen Naletilic, in the way he actually is, the man he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, the problem is that if the interpreters or typists do not make any mistake, we just simply forget them at all. You have plenty of time. Take your time and do it slowly. Yes. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for your understanding. I promised half an hour, so I'm trying to get through it as quickly as possible because I see that I have taken up an hour already. That's why I speeded up. I always seem to be in this -- between a rock and a hard place, between saying what I want to say and saying it in the time that I have at my disposal. But to wind up, Mladen Naletilic had a dream. He dreamt a dream outside Yugoslavia, outside Bosnia-Herzegovina, outside Siroki Brijeg, and outside his Cigansko Brdo hill area. Why? Because he lived as an immigrant in the Federal Republic of Germany. He lived there for 20 years, over 20 years, and that is why he had this dream. He dreamt that one day he would be able to return to his country. And he was thinking of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, a country which he hoped would have the similar type of democracy that he was living in, and that the republics of the former Yugoslavia would be independent states, that the Republic of Croatia would be an independent state of Croats, but also other citizens living within it. And dreaming that dream, he built up a strong, national awareness, national consciousness, but we cannot say that he was a chauvinist. In his world, he found a place for all people, all people who love their own and respect other people's property. After the first multi-party elections, when it was clear that a uni-party system had come to an end and that the rule of communism had come to an end, he went back, convinced that his place was in his native town, his rightful place was in his native town. It was not his will or expectation that a war would break out on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and that what began in a democratic road would end up in bloodshed. Mladen Naletilic did not want to stand by and see his dream disintegrate. He mobilised all his resources and, together with other friends who were the prisoners of consciousness, sets up the Convicts Battalion. As to the young men who joined up, who joined the battalion, he recognised himself from his younger days. He saw himself in them. They were not criminals, as the Prosecution would like to show at all cost, nor were they convicts who had come back from serving a sentence of any kind, but quite the reverse. They were the founding -- founders and members, they were individuals who, through their own convictions, had to go to prison and had to go through legal proceedings, while members who were joining up were, for the most part, young people, very young people, their ages ranging from 18 to 21. And these young people were true to their people and their ideals, loyal to their people and their ideals. Mladen Naletilic was never a member of a single political party. He never had -- held a single political post or office, nor did he take part in any body or organ of power and authority. Neither was he a member of the military hierarchy or military organisation and structure, because -- and that that was so, the Defence will prove, and I'm sure that the Prosecution would have waved documents to that effect long ago, had that been the case. Because nobody can say for himself, "I'm going to be a commander as of tomorrow." He has to be appointed as such by someone, although commanders in the HVO usually functioned in the way that when a village or street was being defended, the most courageous person would become the commander. We are going to show the Court that there were no ranks in the HVO until May of 1994, that is to say after the Washington Agreements. All that existed was an insignia signifying that somebody was a commander from companies and right up to brigades, from squad level to brigade level, and so Judge Clark's question was in order because everybody spoke about commanders. Everybody was a commander, from the lowest unit to the top-most unit, because that was all that existed. This word or term "commander," that was how they were referred to. When the JNA, from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, launched its strong attacks and destructive attacks on Croatia, led by his national feelings and national sentiment, and also by his life's experience, he recognised that this was the beginning of the -- of a war which would come to prevail and take control of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well. The Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina were not militarily organised, nor were they equipped, and my client, Mladen Naletilic, took it upon himself to organise and equip one unit, a single unit. Let me clarify. At the beginning of 1992, during that period of time, let me tell you how the army was organised and created in Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Any person who was of better material standing, or companies which were still not privately owned at the time, they would equip each of their units and then you would have a unit in a factory, in one particular factory, because that factory equipped this unit. You would have the man because the man equipped the unit. He came by the uniforms and weapons and so on. And you would have funny situations, because they wouldn't listen to anybody except the person who actually equipped the unit. So I'm talking about 1991 in Croatia, the beginning of 1992 in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm talking about that period of time. And I'm just trying to conjure up the situation for you, what it was like at the time. Because you come from the well-to-do strata of age-old democracies, and you did not experience a war of this kind. It is difficult to experience it even by looking at the screens, let alone in the courtroom. And so also my client, Mladen Naletilic, came from a good life that he lived in the Federal Republic of Germany. He too had come in from abroad. And he went through an intimate drama of his own, which I will not recount here. I'll wait for a more opportune moment and do so through witnesses in due course. It was, in fact, the disintegration of his family - that was what it was about - precisely because he decided to go to war, or rather to return to Croatia or rather Bosnia. And so it was that he prepared and organised this one, single, solitary unit. He himself was never a soldier personally. He didn't even do his military service in the Yugoslav People's Army. He had no military training or military knowledge. All he had was a heart beating for his people. That is quite certain. His heart was, in fact, too big. And we are going to say so loud and clear - I don't see why not; it is correct - that Mladen Naletilic mobilised and financed the Convicts Battalion, but while it numbered 20 members, which is how many there actually were at the beginning - I'm talking about the beginning of 1992 - those 20 young men - unfortunately, very few of them remain living today - were ready for the defence. It is true that Mladen Naletilic led them in that war against the JNA in 1992. It is also true that because of that, he was celebrated as the liberator of Mostar in that year of 1992 because it is those young men who showed themselves -- proved themselves to be exceptionally brave and were the linchpin of the joint forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO in liberating territory from Mostar right until -- right up until Nevesinje. And then the 18.000 refugees and displaced persons came from those regions at the beginning of the conflict with the JNA, those people who came could go back to their homes, and this was the first major victory in the entire war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And so, at the end of that war, the name of Tuta meant more than Mladen Naletilic. It took on a special meaning, which we could interpret and translate in the following way: as a small people, poorly armed, but with a strong feeling of their own ground, territory, can conquer an enemy a hundred times more powerful. And we can also put it that way: The name of Tuta meant a resistance, it meant a force, a strength, it meant courage, bravery, but also security. It inspired security and safety. And you will hear witnesses in this courtroom who will tell you that in 1992, they felt safe only if they knew that Didjer [phoen] was close by, Didjer and Tuta - and you will hear this from the members of all the ethnic groups - in that year, 1992. Mladen Naletilic, and we as his Defence team, are fully conscious of the fact that his name has been abused. We are -- Mladen Naletilic is conscious of the fact that those people who said they were his friends were not, or are no longer, his friends. Mladen Naletilic himself is fully conscious of the fact that in this courtroom, through force of circumstance, based on many things, but quite certainly not on his criminal responsibility and accountability. The Defence will present evidence to prove this to this Honourable Trial Chamber. And we won't ask for any mercy. We won't seek mercy. We will try and prove the truth, prove what actually happened, and will never be ashamed to say where we were and what we were. And I'm speaking in our joint name. We will stress that with honour and pride. And we never committed crimes. Quite the reverse, quite the contrary. We didn't want to come here and cry and by doing so mask the facts, which is what we see here very frequently around us. This is a court of law. It is a war crimes tribunal and not a committee for political conciliation. And we will indeed only deal with the facts - let me repeat for the hundredth time - the truth as it was, because we do not have anything to hide, and we do not have anything to be ashamed of. That is certain. Had there been a little more goodwill - and I don't know why this was lacking, why this was not so - had my learned colleagues, my learned and distinguished colleagues sitting across the well from me, had they just been a little more objective, my client would never be here in the first place. And when we're talking about justice, Your Honours, justice is partially blind. Anybody can close one eye, at least when it comes to a world court of law, because in this court of law, we are trying just one small point on the globe, and that small point, dot, is called the former Yugoslavia, while other criminals roam around that same globe unfettered. Nobody can do anything to them. So until justice is equal for one and all from American generals to Tajikistan, only then can we say that the scales of justice are equal for all and that justice is not -- does not have a blind eye. That is why the nation to whom -- to which I belong, the people in Croatia, are suspicious of this Tribunal, because crimes take part in different corners of the globe every day and we see them televised on television. But we say to them, and we are trying to convince them that we should have trust in this Tribunal. It is a new institution which has just started to work. And my client, and I too, rely upon your sense of justice. And we shall accept all of your decisions and judgements, whatever they might be. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your eloquent statement. I believe we have to have a break at this moment. And after the break, we'll have the first witness, which we'll do his testimony in closed session. I hope that the registrar will make the proper arrangement for that sitting. We'll resume at twenty -- at twenty to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I thought at this time that there were a few matters I should deal with, both at the closing of the opening statement and prior to the first witness. I'll try to be brief. I feel perhaps, Your Honour, that I should make some record, if you will, in terms of the opening statement, only briefly. It's never exactly clear or -- strike that, not never but it's sometimes not clear what the rules and practices of this International Tribunal are, and they do vary from Chamber to Chamber at times. And I do not want -- I would not want anything said in the opening statement to be taken as given or not disputed by either the lack of objection during the opening statement or now. As the Chamber knows - and I would ask you to tell me if the Chamber is -- I would ask -- appreciate the Chamber's guidance if the Chamber has a different view - as the -- I believe the Chamber knows, of course, the opening statement, just as with a Prosecution opening statement, is not evidence. There were certainly many, many points that will be heavily contested, certainly are not conceded. Largely out of a courtesy of course to Mr. Krsnik, I did not interrupt, I don't think, one time in the two days, but certainly that should not be taken as indicating any sort of agreement with a vast number of assertions that were made. In our view - and again I'm not going to belabour it now - but I will also indicate many parts, many issues that were raised are not relevant to the case. Mr. Krsnik a few times very specifically turned to me and to the Prosecution table and said, "Don't raise tu quoque," and, Your Honours, we may very well -- we will object, we do intend and do anticipate objecting to anything that is tu quoque, just as one example. So I just want to make again those brief comments. Further, picking up once again on Mr. Krsnik's assurances to all of us and to the Chamber that he has nothing to hide, the Prosecution again asks on the record for full disclosure from the Defence, including any witness statements and including all exhibits. Thirdly, there seemed -- we seemed to hear -- the Prosecution seemed to hear something that sounded an awful lot like an alibi defence concern Sovici, that Mr. Naletilic was somewhere else with family members at the time that the -- at least the opening parts of Sovici was taking place. I might remind the Chamber respectfully of Rule 67(A)(2)(a) which requires notice of an alibi defence to be given prior to the commencement of the trial. I would also want to raise primarily this, Your Honours: There is a pending motion from the Defence for the disclosure of any statements that the Prosecution may have concerning Defence witnesses. Now, we have not filed a response to that, nor have we fully -- to be very candid, fully come to terms with what our response will be. Our preliminary assessment -- I think I can say our preliminary view is that we are not aware of any bases in the rules for such a response -- or such a requirement, excuse me. And we will file a written response to that motion. However, because the next witness, the first witness, is about to be called, and out of an abundance of fairness, there is a statement of [redacted] which we will make available to the Defence at this time, without prejudice - and I want to stress this, without prejudice - to our taking the position that in fact the Defence would not be entitled to such material.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, we did not get interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting you. I would just like to ask for these names not to be mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Krsnik may have said -- I apologise, and I would ask for redaction because counsel may have said -- and if he didn't say, I'll raise it myself. I, like many of us, appear to have trouble with this this morning. I did mention a name and I ask that be redacted in line 12. My apology. We do have a statement of a witness, and we will provide that to Defence counsel for both teams at this time, but again, as I started to say, I will do that without prejudice, in our view, to our position that such disclosure may not be in fact required at all. We are doing it out of courtesy and to move forward, without committing to necessarily doing that in the future. So I will tender those statements to counsel at the conclusion of my remarks. Mr. President, it would assist us in planning -- it has not been entirely clear to the Prosecution over the past two days, what the normal break schedule will be during these morning sessions, how many breaks will we take, when will we take them, and for how long. It would assist probably everyone, including the Defence, to know what the Court's anticipated schedule will be. I have noticed in the last two days the Chamber has been taking a half-hour break about every hour. I don't know if you intend to continue with that practice or if there was something exceptional about that. But we would be very appreciative to have the Chamber's additional guidance on that, again for planning purposes for everyone. And finally, Your Honour, I believe I then will let Mr. Stringer address another important witness matter that's come to our attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could I make an initial response to your remarks concerning the opening statement? It is our view that the opening statement is just a summary of the case presented by either the Prosecution or the Defence counsel. It is just a one-sided view, which supplies the views from one party. Certainly they are not evidence at all. They just give the judges certain ideas about their case. And in the normal practice, the opening statement is not arguable, which is -- which means that there should be no interruptions or some debates concerning of the contents of the opening statement. The next issue is about the alibi matters. If the Defence counsel would like to provide the Defence of alibi, they should abide by the Rule 67, which means that they have the responsibility to furnish all those evidence beforehand to the other side. Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. This -- my remarks will relate to an upcoming Defence witness who is requesting protective measures. And it would be my suggestion that we move into private session so that I can inform the Trial Chamber of the issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Will you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, good day. You should be shown by the usher a name, a first and last name, on this piece of paper and the pseudonym we will use for you in this Trial Chamber, but could you please just confirm that this is your first and last name? But don't say it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, we will soon start our examination. I would like to ask you to relax. I know that you are in an unusual situation. Just relax. You may be very tired, or if you get very tired, please tell us if you need a pause, if you need a break. We are mindful of the fact that you are slightly older. If you need water or anything, or if you don't feel good, feel free to say so. We shall accept that, of course. The first question I would like to ask you is - I think we can start now, don't mention your name but could you please introduce yourself to this Trial Chamber, in a few sentences tell us when you were born, which schools you went to, when you retired, et cetera. So please just introduce yourself briefly to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA
utterances.text: I was born on the 12th of February, 1927, in Vitina the municipality of Ljubuski, which is in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I finished primary school in the place of my birth. I finished secondary school in Zagreb. I went to the second classical gymnasium. I studied law in Zagreb, and I graduated in 1965. I did post-graduate studies at the department of economy -- at the economic university in Zagreb, and I obtained my Masters in 1974. From 1961, I worked in many companies in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I retired in 1989. And then in the second half of that year, in the second half of 1990, I became active in political life in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I joined the Croatian Democratic Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Boras, I just wanted a short curriculum vitae at the beginning. We shall continue to talk about these events now. I would like to ask you, could you tell this Trial Chamber what were the reasons for which you asked for a closed session.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA
utterances.text: For many reasons, but I shall mention only a few. I'm a public personality. I have a large family. My daughter, my son-in-law, my children were expelled from Zenica. They have the intention, at least for the moment, and they are conducting proceedings -- they are engaged in proceedings to obtain their flat back, to get their flat back, a flat which was completely destroyed. But nevertheless, if they manage to get it back and if they could get -- get back the jobs that they were dismissed from before at the beginning of 1994, if they could get this back, then they would probably return. Furthermore, my wife's sister and her family live in Zenica. My wife's brother and her family also live in Zenica. I think these sufficient reasons for a closed session. This is why I asked for a closed session. And I thank the Trial Chamber for allowing me -- it to be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, your daughter and son-in-law, were they exchanged? Was there an exchange of civilians or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA
utterances.text: Yes. In an exchange of soldiers, the brother of a prominent commander in the 7th Muslim Brigade in Zenica, who later became the commander of the 4th Corps of the BH army in Mostar. His name is Brzina, Halil. His brother was exchanged for my family. I don't know his -- his name, but it's Brzina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. So we shall carry on with our work. I'm going to ask you some questions. Could you please just wait to hear the English translation over the earphones, wait for the interpreters to interpret everything, to translate everything, and then we shall start talking. I'd be grateful for this. My first question is: Could you tell the Trial Chamber what the constitutional order was in the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia in 1990 and just before all those events that transpired in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA
utterances.text: The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I apologise. Are you sure it's the federal? I said the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA
utterances.text: The Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was a federal state with -- federal state with six republics, and it had two autonomous republics -- I'm sorry, provinces within the Socialist Republic of Serbia. And the federal institutions had an assembly, they had a presidency, a government, and other things, a federal court, a constitutional court, and everything else that is required by such a constitutional order in such a country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Sorry. If I can just interrupt you for a minute. Was the model at the federal level also applied at the republican level?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA
utterances.text: The model was almost identical. It was parallel to that model. It was perhaps -- it was even identical, so that the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina had its own assembly, its own government, its own presidency. It had its constitutional court, supreme court. It had its national bank. But these were all formal institutions. However, since it was a one-party system -- a single-party system - there was the League of Communists of Yugoslavia and the League of Communists of the republics - the government was sort of duplicated. The informal party government was duplicated, since they would appoint personnel into these official institutions, to the government, to the assemblies, to the presidency, and they would do this on the base of the suggestions from the central committees, on the base of their proposal. So it would be possible to say given that power, as they would say, was in the hands of the proletariat, and the proletariat through the dictatorship of the proletariat in fact governed social life as a whole in Yugoslavia and in the individual republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What do you know about the organisation -- and you just mentioned a few details -- about the organisation in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina? I'm thinking about the social/political organisation and the army there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA
utterances.text: I said that all the institutions in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina were like those in the other republics and also at the level of Yugoslavia. But in 1990, from Croatia and Slovenia, and before that with the fall of the Berlin Wall, with the disintegration of the Soviet Union, democratic changes were initiated --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I would like to interrupt you at this point. I wanted to ask you about this, but you've already started to talk about this. I'm not sure if this is what you were going to say. But what do you know about how the multiparty system was introduced into Bosnia and Herzegovina? Perhaps you could say which party you were a member of, if you were a member of a party, and how the parties were formed, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA
utterances.text: Well, in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- Bosnia-Herzegovina could simply not follow the democratic movements which had started in Slovenia and in Croatia subsequently, and Serbia too and Montenegro. By the middle of 1990, they even had their own state, although it was still within the framework of Yugoslavia. But all the institutions -- Mr. Milosevic had already formed all the institutions, and they were directed toward this goal, an independent state, and this is what Croatia and Slovenia were tending towards. In August, the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina issued certain rules, certain laws, according to which it was possible to introduce a multiparty system. And it was not until the beginning of October in 1990 the last rule was adopted by the assembly, and it concerned the constitution of the presidency. And this last change which was brought about, it involved the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There were seven members, two members from each people and one member from the other peoples, the Yugoslavs, the Roma, and other ethnic minorities. So that with these regulations, it was made possible for individual parties to appear. And they had already started appearing. And the party which was for the Croatian people, on behalf of the Croatian people, also appeared. This party was the Croatian Democratic Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly, please, what you know about what the major parties were? Which parties won the first multi-party elections, in fact, and when did they take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA
utterances.text: The first multi-party elections, according to a decision taken by the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, were held on the 18th of November, 1990. The voters voted in the national parties: The Croatian Democratic Union, and the Croatian electorate voted for them; the Serbian Democratic Party got the votes of the Serb electorate; and the Party of Democratic Action won the votes of the Muslim people. There were several other parties, such as the Reformists, the Reformist Party. They won a smaller number of votes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting but could you explain to the Trial Chamber what these Reformist -- who these Reformists were? What was their programme and platform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA
utterances.text: The Reformist Party, or the Reformists, were in fact made up of the former premier, Ante Markovic. He formed the Reformist Party when the elections were last in the Socialist Republic of Serbia, Slovenia and Croatia, that is to say when the League of Communists lost the elections there. That is when, especially for Bosnia-Herzegovina, the former Prime Minister, whose name was Ante Markovic, formed the Reformist Party in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they won about 10 per cent of the votes in the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know who the President of the party was for Bosnia-Herzegovina? Do you happen to know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA
utterances.text: That was university professor Nenad Kecmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: On the basis of what population census in Bosnia-Herzegovina were the elections organised? Or rather, how were the elections organised? Could you tell us a little about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA
utterances.text: The population census for the electoral body -- the last census actually was taken, being in 1981 -- 1991, that is to say, after the elections. There was a census after the elections. And that one couldn't be taken into account, so the 1981 population census was taken to be the basis for the elections. And the voting was for the assembly, and it had two chambers, the Chamber of Citizens and the Chamber of Municipalities. And elections took place simultaneously both for the municipality bodies and for the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you happen to know the results of the elections for the presidency and who they were? The number of votes, if you happen to know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA
utterances.text: Well, although I can't give you any exact figures, the largest number of votes was secured by Fikret Abdic, leading the Party of Democratic Action. He got about 1.400.000 votes or 44 per cent of the overall electoral body. Next came Alija Izetbegovic. He won about 850 odd or 870.000 votes. The third -- third place, as far as I remember, went to Durakovic, who was the President of the League of Communists, and the SDP party of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He won about 510.000 votes. And the two of us, that is to say representatives of the Croatian people, or rather the HDZ party, Mr. Kljujic won 470.000 votes and I myself secured 416.000 votes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Before I show you a map or chart, let me ask you, was there any agreement? Did the parties give instructions to their electorate as to the voting procedure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA
utterances.text: Yes. There was a special agreement between the SDA and the HDZ, for example. And the agreement was to the effect that the electoral body of Croatia, or rather the HDZ electoral body should vote for representatives in the presidency - and I'm now speaking about the presidency - should vote for representatives of the SDA party, for presidency members in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and vice versa, that the electoral body of the SDA party voting for Fikret Abdic, Alija Izetbegovic and Ganic on behalf of the other peoples, should vote for me and for Kljujic reciprocally. However, we were let down by the SDA, headed by Alija Izetbegovic, just before the elections took place, say four or five days before the elections. They took the vertical line from Sarajevo at the top, right down to the smallest place down at the bottom. They instructed their electoral body, their voters, not to vote for me or for Kljujic but to vote for the other Croatian members from the other parties, such as, for example, Ivo Komesic was put forward on behalf of the League of Communists, for example, and the SDP also put forward a candidate for presidency member. Now, what happened? Had they adhered to the agreement that had been reached previously, both I, myself and Kljujic should have won the same number of votes as Fikret Abdic, because we carried out an analysis on one occasion, in Mostar actually, in a suburb of Mostar, with an exclusively -- which is an exclusively Croatian-populated area, with about 100 voters of Muslim -- the Muslim ethnic -- Muslim ethnicity. And what happened? In that almost completely Croatian-inhabited -- populated area, Fikret Abdic and Alija Izetbegovic got more votes than I and Kljujic received. Why? Because the Croats all voted for me and Kljujic and also voted for Alija and Fikret Abdic, whereas the Muslims only voted for Fikret Abdic and Alija Izetbegovic. And that's what happened at the level of the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The situation was mirrored.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know that -- whether had the Croats not abided by the agreement, would Alija Izetbegovic have secured sufficient votes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA
utterances.text: No. Without the Croatian votes Alija Izetbegovic would not have become a member of the presidency but that would have been the former president of the central committee of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, and he was Nijaz Durakovic. He would have won.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: All right. Well, the elections were over. The presidency was elected. Can you now tell us a little bit about something that the Defence considers to be particularly important, in order to explain and clarify what happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina later on, how the new government was constituted, how the presidency was constituted, what your tasks were? But before you go on to do so, I should like to ask the usher's assistance, please. Would he please place this photograph on the ELMO? And it is Defence Exhibit D1/48. Can you tell us whether you're familiar with this photograph, and if so, who is on it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA
utterances.text: Yes. These are members of the presidency photographed when they were taking their oath of office on the 20th of December, 1990. Let me start -- move from left to right, go from left to right: Mr. Ganic; next, Mr. Koljevic; this is me; Fikret Abdic; Biljana Plavsic; Alija Izetbegovic; and Stjepan Kljuic. With his back turned towards us is the president of the assembly, Momcilo Krajisnik. And we are taking the oath of office in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, we've said that the elections were held and that the agreement was not adhered to, was not respected. What about Mr. Ganic? Did Mr. Ganic enter the presidency, if I can put it that way, in a legal manner, a legal and lawful manner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA
utterances.text: Mr. Ganic at that time was a citizen of Yugoslavia. Now, whether he had the right to be a candidate for a member of the Bosnia-Herzegovina presidency, I can't say, because at that time you could be a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina and of Yugoslavia as well, two citizenships. Now, the constitution or constitutional experts dealt with the matter, I assume, so I assume that he did have the right. He probably could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But as he was an SDA member and represented the Yugoslavs, by that virtue --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA
utterances.text: Oh, well, yes, that's another problem. As soon as he became a member of the presidency, he forgot all the rest, all the others that had actually elected him, and he joined up with and became a member of the SDA party, and Alija Izetbegovic had an enormous amount of confidence in him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you tell this Trial Chamber - I'll try and take things in their order, chronological order - what happened on the 6th of May at Polog in Mostar 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA
utterances.text: A tank brigade that was -- had previously been stationed in Mostar set out via Siroki Brijeg towards Kupres allegedly to hold military manoeuvres, exercises. However, the Croatian people of that region saw through the ill intentions of that tank brigade, or rather, the military command of the Yugoslav People's Army, not only in Mostar but also -- but this also came from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could I just interrupt you for a moment, sir. I see in the transcript that it -- this happened on the 6th of May, 1992. Was it the 6th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA
utterances.text: No. It was 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. As to the presidency, if you happen to know - as you were a member, I'm sure you do know this - the Supreme Commander of the army, was there an army in Bosnia-Herzegovina? What about that? Did Bosnia-Herzegovina have its own army of sorts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA
utterances.text: In the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina and pursuant to the federal constitution, the presidency of every republic, which meant the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina itself, was in command of the Territorial Defence forces. It was the Supreme Commander, in fact, the supreme commanding body of the Territorial Defence. However, when we took our positions in the presidency, the democratically elected government that we were, already at that time the Territorial Defence had been disbanded and the weapons had been confiscated, and those weapons had previously been bought by the municipalities and socially owned companies and even citizens gave their own contributions in terms of funds to purchase weapons and to have the people armed, because that was the concept of total national defence against the foreign enemy, a foreign foe, in case of war. If the external borders of Yugoslavia were to be attacked, the whole population would have been mobilised. So in addition to the Yugoslav People's Army, Tito proclaimed the formation of a Territorial Defence force, which included each and every citizen -- able-bodied citizen from the ages of 16 to 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I think our time is up for today. I see that it is already quarter to 2.00, so we'll have to end there for today and continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have made note of the time, and I see that it is a quarter to 2.00. With your permission, I take it that we can conclude for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, I'm afraid that we have to call you back tomorrow morning. So during your stay in The Hague, as I did with other witnesses, I have to warn you do not talk to anybody about your testimony and don't let anybody talk to you about it, including the Defence counsels. Usher, would you please show the witness out of the room first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will resume at 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 27th day of March, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
